title: The universe in Krishna's mouth
hookLine: a mother looks into her small son's mouth for dirt and sees everything there is, herself included
carry: vatsalya: loving God as your own child
tomorrow: why didn't the bhakti saints sing in Sanskrit?

cards: The other boys come running to Yashoda with a complaint: Krishna has been eating dirt. She grabs his hand and scolds him. He looks up, all innocence, and says they're lying.
If she doesn't believe him, she can look for herself. So she does the obvious thing. Open your mouth, she says.
He opens it. And she does not find dirt.

teach.h: THE WHOLE WORLD IN A CHILD'S MOUTH.
teach.b: Here is what the Bhagavata Purana says she saw, in paraphrase. Inside the little mouth: the sky in every direction, the mountains, the islands and oceans, the earth, wind and fire, the moon and the stars.
The whole moving world. And inside all of that, the village of Vraja.
And inside the village, herself, standing there, looking into a child's mouth. Yashoda is shaken. The text lets her wonder aloud: is this a dream?
A trick of the gods' illusion? Some power in my own boy?
She bows, in her heart, to the one who holds all of it. Then comes the turn. The text says Krishna spread his maya over her, his power of veiling, in the form of a mother's love.
She forgets what she has seen. She lifts him onto her lap, and he is her son again, a boy who may or may not have eaten dirt. Again and again the Krishna stories hold two things at once.
The child is the whole universe.

teach.h: VATSALYA: GOD LOVED AS A CHILD.
teach.b: The child is also just a child who needs his face washed. Some readers hear Yashoda's forgetting as a gift, not a loss: the ordinary love handed back.
That love has a name in bhakti: vatsalya, loving God the way a parent loves a child. And it is a real way of worship.
In many Hindu homes a small image of the child Krishna, Bal Gopal or Laddu Gopal, is bathed, dressed, fed and put to rest, and at Janmashtami his cradle is rocked.
God, who holds the universe, is let in as someone small to care for.

how: The story of Yashoda seeing the universe in Krishna's mouth is told and sung in homes and temples, painted in miniatures, and retold during Janmashtami; devotees speak of vatsalya, loving God as a parent loves a child, and in many homes a small image of the child Krishna (Bal Gopal, Laddu Gopal) is bathed, dressed, fed and rocked.

o: a vision of the whole universe at once
tender love, like a parent's for a child, offered to God
a child's mischief, like stealing butter

games.q: Yashoda and the open mouth — tap the pairs.
p: veils it as a mother's love

s: Yashoda finds dirt in Krishna's mouth
she finds the whole universe, with the village and herself inside it.
after the vision, Yashoda forgets what she saw
the Bhagavata says Krishna's maya covered her as a mother's love, and she took him on her lap.
the text treats her forgetting as a punishment
the veil that covers the vision is made of a mother's love, not a penalty.

games.q: you are Yashoda. you've just seen the universe inside your son's mouth. what happens next in the text?
o: she tells the whole village what she saw.
she forgets, and takes him on her lap.
she sends him away to the sages.
games.why: after her wonder and her bow, Krishna's maya covers her as motherly love; she forgets the vision and holds her son again.

practice: Let this be a sit in two halves. First, widen: let attention open past the room, to the sky and everything under it, the way Yashoda saw it all at once. Then, halfway, come home.
If you pray, picture the child Krishna, or the form of God you love, as small and near, and offer him something in your mind: a sip of water, a sweet, a blanket.
If you don't, bring to mind a child you have cared for, and stay with that tenderness.

wordCard.voice: Vatsalya. Tender parental love, the veil that let Yashoda hold her son again after she saw the whole universe in his mouth.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: vatsalya, tender parental love; in bhakti, the love Yashoda has for Krishna.
